entry:
Fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the [[Solar System]]. A [[Gas giant|gas giant]], it has a mass nearly 2.5 times that of all the other planets combined and slightly less than one-thousandth that of the Sun, and its diameter is 11 times that of Earth. It orbits the Sun at a distance of 5.20 AU (778.5 Gm) with an orbital period of 11.86 years. It is the third-brightest natural object in Earth's night sky, after the Moon and Venus, and was named after the chief deity of ancient Roman religion.

The atmosphere is 76% [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] and 24% [[Helium|helium]] by mass, with traces of carbon, oxygen, sulfur, neon, ammonia, and water vapor. The outer atmosphere is divided into latitudinal bands, with turbulence and storms along their boundaries; the most obvious result is the [[Great Red Spot]], a giant storm recorded since 1831. Rotating once in about ten hours, it is an oblate spheroid, its equatorial radius about 7% larger than its polar radius. Its interior is believed to consist of an outer mantle of fluid metallic hydrogen and a diffuse inner core of denser material. Its [[Magnetic field|magnetic field]], generated by eddy currents within the fluid metallic hydrogen, is the strongest and second-largest contiguous structure in the Solar System.

At least 115 moons orbit Jupiter. The four largest, Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, are the [[Galilean moons]]; they are visible with common binoculars, and Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury. A faint ring system consists mainly of dust. Since 1973, nine robotic probes have visited the planet: seven flybys and two dedicated orbiters, with two more en route.

Concept of treating individuals fairly, central to morality, law, and political philosophy. A frequently cited core definition comes from the Institutes of Justinian, a 6th-century codification of Roman law: "the constant and perpetual will to render to each his due."

Early Western theories were developed by Greek philosophers. For [[Plato]], in *The Republic*, justice is balance and harmony: everyone having and doing what they are responsible for or what belongs to them. He compared the three parts of a person, reason, spirit, and desire, with the three parts of a city. [[Aristotle]], in the [[Nicomachean Ethics]], treated justice both as nearly synonymous with virtue and as the particular virtue of giving people what they deserve; his particular justice divides into distributive justice, which allocates goods in proportion to merit, and corrective justice, which restores balance after exchanges or harms. The classical Confucian theory treated justice as a personal and public virtue that did not include freedom or equality and was not part of the law.

Modern Western notions have roots in Christian theology and divine command theory, under which God's commands determine morality and therefore justice. In the 17th century, [[John Locke]] held that justice derives from natural law, while [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] advocated social contract theory, in which justice arises from mutual agreement to be governed. Modern frameworks include distributive justice; [[Utilitarianism|utilitarian]] theories, which look to the future consequences of [[Punishment|punishment]]; retributive justice, which matches punishment to past wrongdoing; and restorative justice, which focuses on the needs of victims, offenders, and society. Procedural justice concerns the impartiality of the processes by which outcomes are reached.

German philosopher, social and political theorist, journalist, and revolutionary socialist. Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia to a family of Jewish descent that had converted to Christianity, Marx earned a doctorate in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841. He was influenced by [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel]] and the Young Hegelians, and began a close collaboration with [[Friedrich Engels]] in Paris. With Engels he wrote *The Communist Manifesto* (1848), which lays out a program for revolution. Expelled from Germany after the Revolutions of 1848, he settled in [[London]], where he researched in the British Museum and wrote the *Grundrisse* notebooks and the three volumes of *Das Kapital* (1867–1894). He became a leading figure in the International Workingmen's Association, in which he opposed the anarchists led by Mikhail Bakunin, and celebrated the [[Paris Commune]] of 1871.

Marx developed the theory of historical materialism, holding that societies develop through class conflict. Under [[Capitalism|capitalism]], this is the conflict between the bourgeoisie, who control the means of production, and the proletariat, who sell their labor for wages. Using a dialectical approach, he argued that capital accumulation produces internal contradictions that would lead to the system's self-destruction, and that the working class would then establish a classless, stateless society.

His ideas, collectively called [[Marxism]], inspired revolutionary movements, and Marxism–Leninism became the guiding ideology of states formed in the 20th century. His work is both widely praised and widely criticized. Critics point to the authoritarian outcomes of states founded in his name and to the failure of capitalism to collapse as predicted, while supporters credit his influence on heterodox economics and his role as a principal architect of modern sociology.

Country (pop., mid-2026 est.: more than 54.2 million), East Africa, area 580,367 sq km. The capital and largest city is [[Nairobi]]; the second-largest and oldest is [[Mombasa]], a port on Mombasa Island. Kenya is bordered by South Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, the Indian Ocean, Tanzania, and Uganda, and shares Lake Victoria with its western neighbors. Its landscape ranges from snow-capped peaks on [[Mount Kenya]], which at 5,199 m is Africa's second-highest, to arid and semi-arid regions and deserts such as the Chalbi.

Some of the earliest humans evolved in Kenya, and fossils have been found at Koobi Fora. In 1984, near [[Lake Turkana]], Richard Leakey and Kamoya Kimeu found the Turkana Boy, a 1.6-million-year-old [[Homo erectus]] fossil. Cushitic speakers settled the lowlands between 3,200 and 1,300 BC, Nilotic-speaking pastoralists began arriving around 500 BC, and Bantu people settled between 250 BC and AD 500. European contact began in 1500 with the Portuguese. A protectorate was established by the [[British Empire]] in 1895, and the Kenya Colony began in 1920. After the Mau Mau revolution, which began in 1952, independence was declared on December 12, 1963, and Kenya remained in the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

Kenya is a presidential representative democratic republic; William Ruto took office as president in September 2022. Its economy, the largest in East and Central Africa, is lower-middle-income, with a per-capita gross national income of $2,110. Agriculture is the largest sector, with tea and coffee as traditional cash crops and fresh flowers a fast-growing export; tourism is also a major driver. Kenya belongs to the UN, the East African Community, and the [[International Monetary Fund]], among other bodies, and hosts the headquarters of the United Nations Environment Programme.

Tool or weapon with a cutting edge or blade, usually attached to a handle or hilt. Knives are among the earliest tools used by humanity, appearing at least 2.5 million years ago, as evidenced by Oldowan tools. They were originally made of wood, bone, and stone such as flint and [[Obsidian|obsidian]]; with advances in metallurgy and manufacturing, blades came to be made of copper, [[Bronze|bronze]], iron, [[Steel|steel]], ceramic, and titanium.

A modern knife consists of a blade and a handle. The blade has a point, an edge (plain, serrated, or both), a grind (its cross-section shape), and a spine. The handle may include a tang extending into it, partial or full, as well as a bolster and a guard that protects the hand.

Blade materials have differing advantages. Carbon steel, an alloy of iron and carbon, takes a very sharp edge and is easy to sharpen but is vulnerable to rust and stains. [[Stainless steel]] contains chromium, possibly nickel and molybdenum, and little carbon; it takes a slightly less sharp edge but resists corrosion. [[Titanium]] has a higher strength-to-weight ratio and is more flexible than steel but is less hard. [[Ceramic|Ceramic]] blades are hard, brittle, lightweight, and noncorroding; they hold an edge for years but break if dropped or twisted. Steel blades are shaped by [[Forging|forging]], in which a heated piece is hammered or pressed, or by stock removal, in which metal is ground away; both methods are followed by heat treatment.

Knives serve many purposes, from hunting, combat, and camping to kitchen work (the chef's knife, paring knife, bread knife, and cleaver), table use, throwing, and religious ceremony or display, such as the *kirpan*. Weapons include the [[Dagger|dagger]] and the switchblade.

Awareness of facts (descriptive knowledge), familiarity with individuals and situations (knowledge by acquaintance), or practical skill (procedural knowledge). Descriptive knowledge, also called propositional knowledge, is often characterized as true belief distinguished from opinion or guesswork by justification. Philosophers widely agree that propositional knowledge is a form of true belief, but controversies surround justification: how to understand it, whether it is needed at all, and whether something besides it is needed. It is closely related to intelligence, which concerns the ability to acquire, process, and apply information, whereas knowledge concerns information and skills a person already possesses.

The English word comes from the 12th-century Old English *cnawan*. Ancient Greek used four important terms: *epistēmē* (unchanging theoretical knowledge), *technē* (expert technical knowledge), *mētis* (strategic knowledge), and *gnōsis* (personal intellectual knowledge).

The main discipline investigating knowledge is [[Epistemology|epistemology]], which studies what people know, how they come to know it, and what it means to know something. It also considers the value of knowledge and philosophical skepticism, which questions whether knowledge is possible.

A long-discussed definition, which has roots in [[Plato]]'s exploration of the question, treats knowledge as justified true belief. Truth is a widely accepted feature, since one cannot know something false. Justification is included because some true beliefs, such as lucky guesses or beliefs based on superstition or erroneous reasoning, do not seem to be knowledge. Some philosophers hold that a belief is justified if it rests on evidence; others hold that it is justified if produced by a reliable process, such as sensory perception or logical reasoning.

In 1963, Edmund Gettier presented counterexamples of justified true beliefs that fail to constitute knowledge because of epistemic luck. In a well-known example, a driver in a country with many barn facades and one real barn stops by chance in front of the real barn and believes it is a barn; the belief is justified and true, yet the driver could not have told the difference. Such cases prompted alternative definitions, including reliabilism.

Knowledge can be produced in many ways. The main source of empirical knowledge is [[Perception|perception]], the use of the senses to learn about the external world. [[Introspection]] reveals one's own mental states and processes. Other sources include [[Memory|memory]], rational intuition, [[Inference|inference]], and testimony. According to foundationalism, some sources are basic and can justify beliefs without depending on other mental states. Coherentists hold that a sufficient degree of coherence among all of a believer's mental states is necessary, and infinitism holds that an infinite chain of beliefs is needed.

Knowledge is relevant to many fields. The sciences aim to acquire it through the [[Scientific method|scientific method]], based on repeatable experimentation, observation, and measurement. Various religions hold that humans should seek knowledge and that God or the divine is its source. The anthropology of knowledge studies how it is acquired, stored, retrieved, and communicated across cultures, and the [[Sociology|sociology]] of knowledge examines the circumstances in which it arises.

Port city (pop., November 2025 est.: 17–21 million), southwestern [[Nigeria]], and the country's largest city. It is the most populous urban area in Africa and one of the fastest-growing megacities in the world. Its Yoruba name is Èkó. The name derives from the Portuguese word for "lakes."

The city lies on creeks and islands at the southwest mouth of Lagos Lagoon, protected from the [[Atlantic Ocean]] by barrier islands and sand spits. The Island of Lagos emerged in the 15th century as a home of the Awori, a subgroup of the [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]]. Britain annexed Lagos in 1861, and it served as capital of colonial Nigeria from 1914 and as the national capital after independence in 1960. In February 1976 the government decided to move the capital to [[Abuja]], and the seat of government officially relocated on December 12, 1991. Lagos State was created in 1967; the city proper consists of 16 local government areas, including Ikeja, the state capital.

Lagos has an international airport, three ports (Apapa, Tin Can Island, and Lekki deep-sea port), and four expressways, and it handles 88% of Nigeria's exports. It is the leading financial center of [[West Africa]] and Central Africa and home to the Nigerian Exchange Group, the main stock exchange group in Nigeria. Other employers include breweries, shipyards, and the Dangote Refinery, and five of seven African technology start-ups valued above US$1 billion are located there.

Lagos is a cultural hub. It is the center of Nigerian cinema, known as Nollywood, and a hub of Afrobeats music. Despite its economic weight, it is strained by infrastructure deficits, including long commutes, housing shortages, and unreliable power and sanitation.

Relatively large, fixed body of water in a basin on or near the Earth's surface, surrounded by dry land and separate from the ocean. Lakes are part of the [[Water cycle|water cycle]]. Most are fresh water and hold almost all the world's surface freshwater, but some are salt lakes with salinities even higher than seawater. In total they cover approximately 2.5 × 10⁶ sq km, less than 2% of Earth's surface.

The word comes from Middle English *lake*, from Old English *lacu* ("pond, pool, stream"). Lakes are typically larger and deeper than [[Pond|ponds]], but neither term has an internationally accepted definition; proposed minimum sizes range from 2 to 8 hectares, and the ecologist Charles Elton regarded lakes as bodies of 40 hectares or more. Lakes also differ from [[Lagoon|lagoons]], which are shallow tidal pools dammed by sandbars or similar material on coasts. Most lakes are fed by springs, precipitation, and runoff, and most have a natural outflow that maintains the average level. Endorheic lakes have no outflow and lose water only by evaporation or seepage.

Natural lakes are generally found in mountainous areas, dormant volcanic craters, rift zones, and areas of ongoing glaciation. Most lakes lie in the Northern Hemisphere at higher latitudes. [[Canada]] has an estimated 31,752 lakes larger than 3 sq km, and at least 2 million in total; Finland has 168,000 lakes of 500 sq m or more. On a geologic time scale, every lake has a finite lifetime, as it will eventually fill with [[Sediment|sediment]] or spill out of its basin.

Artificially controlled lakes are called [[Reservoir|reservoirs]], built for hydroelectric power, drinking water, industry, agriculture, aquaculture, or recreation. The [[Great Lakes]] of North America together hold about 21% of the world's surface freshwater, roughly 22,671 cubic km.

Solid terrestrial surface of Earth not submerged by the ocean or another body of water, also called dry land or ground. It makes up approximately 29% of Earth's surface and includes all continents and islands. It is almost entirely covered by regolith, a layer of rock, soil, and minerals forming the outer part of the crust. One-third of land is covered in trees, another third is used for [[Agriculture|agriculture]], and roughly one-tenth is covered in glacier ice; the remainder is desert, savanna, and prairie. About 30% has a dry climate. The word may also mean the natural resources land holds, including rivers, lakes, and the biosphere, and human modifications such as agriculture and architecture. The boundary between land and sea is the shoreline.

The word derives from Old English, from Proto-Germanic *landą*, "untilled land." Many place names end in *-land*, as in England, Greenland, and New Zealand; the Indo-Iranian equivalent *-stan* appears in Pakistan, Afghanistan, and elsewhere in Central Asia.

The earliest material found in the Solar System dates to 4.5672 ± 0.0006 billion years ago, and the primordial Earth had formed by 4.54 ± 0.04 billion years ago. Earth's atmosphere and oceans formed through volcanic outgassing, and the crust formed when the molten outer layer cooled. Continents are formed by [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]], driven by the loss of heat from Earth's interior. Over hundreds of millions of years, supercontinents have formed and broken apart three times: Rodinia began to break apart roughly 750 million years ago, the continents recombined as Pannotia 600–540 million years ago, and then as [[Pangaea]], which broke apart 180 million years ago.

A continuous area of land surrounded by ocean is a landmass. There are four major landmasses: Africa–Eurasia, America, Antarctica, and Australia. They are subdivided into up to seven continents, which in order of land area are Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia. In physical geology, land divides into mountain ranges and relatively flat interiors called cratons, both formed over millions of years. Streams shape the landscape, carve rocks, transport sediments, and replenish groundwater. At high elevations or latitudes, snow compacts into [[Glacier|glaciers]], which can be heavy enough to warp the crust. Terrain affects travel, mapmaking, ecosystems, and surface water flow, and it largely determines suitability for human settlement.

Earth's first cellular life likely originated on land, and biodiversity then evolved over hundreds of millions of years, interrupted by mass extinctions. Survival on land depends on fresh water, which constitutes only 3% of Earth's water. The study of land in general is geography; mineralogy studies minerals, petrology studies rocks, and soil science studies soils, including pedology (soil formation) and edaphology (the relationship between soil and life). In recent decades, scientists and policymakers have emphasized managing land more sustainably by restoring degraded soil, preserving biodiversity, protecting endangered species, and addressing climate change.

Structured system of communication consisting of grammar and vocabulary. It is the primary means by which humans convey meaning, in spoken and signed forms and through writing. Human languages are culturally and historically diverse and share the properties of productivity, which allows an infinite number of sentences, and displacement, the ability to refer to objects, events, and ideas not immediately present. Use of language relies on social convention, and it is acquired through learning. A 2026 estimate put the number of spoken or signed languages remaining at around 7,500, half of them described as endangered. Precise counts depend on an arbitrary distinction between languages and dialects. Academic consensus holds that between 50% and 90% of the languages spoken at the beginning of the 21st century will probably be extinct by 2100.

The English word derives from Proto-Indo-European through Latin *lingua*, "language; tongue," and Old French *language*. The term also covers constructed systems such as computer languages. Natural language is modality-independent: it can be spoken, signed, or encoded in writing, whistling, or braille. All languages rely on semiosis, the relating of signs to meanings. Oral, manual, and tactile languages contain a phonological system governing how symbols form words or morphemes, and a syntactic system governing how these combine into phrases and utterances. The Swiss linguist [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] distinguished *langage* (language as a concept), *langue* (a specific language system), and *parole* (concrete speech).

The scientific study of language is [[Linguistics|linguistics]]. Debates about its nature and origin go back to the ancient world: Gorgias argued that language could represent neither objective nor human experience, while [[Plato]] held that communication is possible because language represents ideas that exist independently of it. During the Enlightenment, [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] and Johann Gottfried Herder argued that language originated in the instinctive expression of emotion and was originally closer to music and poetry, whereas rationalists such as [[Immanuel Kant]] and René Descartes held the opposite view. In the 20th century, [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] and others associated with the linguistic turn argued that philosophy is essentially the study of language.

Language is thought to have diverged gradually from primate communication systems when early hominins acquired the ability to form a theory of mind and shared intentionality, perhaps coinciding with an increase in brain volume. It is processed in many parts of the brain, especially Broca's and Wernicke's areas. Children acquire it through social interaction and generally speak fluently by about three years old. Language and culture are codependent, and language also signifies group identity and social stratification and serves for social grooming and entertainment.

Languages evolve and diversify. A group descended from a common ancestor is a [[Language family|language family]]; a language with no demonstrated relationship to any other is an isolate.
